title: Kedoshim: the corners of the field (Leviticus 19:9–10)
hookLine: leave the field's edges and fallen grapes for the poor and the stranger

cards: A field of barley at harvest, gold to the edges. The owner planted it, waited on the rain, and counts every stalk as his. The harvesters are swinging their sickles toward the far end.
In the Book of Ruth, a young widow from Moab, poor and far from home, walks into a field like this one, behind the harvesters, and starts picking up what they drop. Nobody chases her off.
Because the owner of the field had been told, long before, to leave her something.

teach.b: Leviticus 19 says: when you reap, don't reap the corner of your field all the way. That corner is called pe'ah, the edge. Don't go back for the gleanings, the stalks that drop as you cut.
In the vineyard, don't strip every last cluster, and don't pick up the fallen grapes.
The reason, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation: "thou shalt leave them for the poor and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God." How big a corner? The Torah doesn't say.
The Mishnah opens its tractate on the subject with a list of things that have no fixed measure, and pe'ah is first on the list, next to acts of kindness and Torah study.
Then the rabbis set a floor: at least one sixtieth of the field. And a detail about dignity: the owner doesn't hand the corner out to people he likes.
It's left standing, and those in need come and harvest it themselves, waiting on nobody's favor. Then the story it made possible.

teach.h: RUTH IN THE FIELD OF BOAZ.
teach.b: Ruth, gleaning, ends up in the field of Boaz, a relative of her mother-in-law Naomi's late husband.

He tells his workers to let some stalks fall on purpose for her. Their marriage, the Book of Ruth says, leads to King David. A line of kings, traced back to a field where the poor were allowed to gather.

how: Farmers in Israel who keep the agricultural laws still leave pe'ah, and some Jews outside farming see tzedakah, giving to those in need, as continuing the same commandment; the Mishnah's tractate Peah, which opens with the list of things without measure, is recited in the morning prayers.

o: a harvest festival held at summer's end
a tenth of the harvest given to the priests
the corner of a field left for the poor

games.q: what's inside the field — tap the pairs.
p: gleaned in the field of Boaz

s: the Torah says exactly how big the corner must be
it doesn't. the Mishnah lists pe'ah first among things with no fixed measure; the rabbis set a minimum of one sixtieth.
the poor harvested the corner themselves
the owner doesn't choose who gets it. they come and gather.
Ruth's gleaning leads, in the story, to King David
she marries Boaz, and the Book of Ruth traces David from them.

games.q: you own the field. it's harvest, and a poor stranger is following your workers, picking up what drops. what does Leviticus 19 have you do?
o: send her away; the field is yours.
leave the corners and the fallen stalks for her.
games.why: leave them for the poor and the stranger. Boaz went further: he had his workers drop stalks on purpose for Ruth.

practice: Think about the fields of your own life: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, your space.

Where could you leave an edge uncut, not a big donation but a corner: the last good parking spot, part of a bonus, an hour of your week, food left at a pantry box without needing to see who takes it? Let one corner come to mind.

wordCard.voice: Pe'ah. The corner of the field left unharvested, so the poor and the stranger can come and gather for themselves.

orig.note: Hebrew: edge, corner: the part of the field left for the poor (Leviticus 19:9).

carryVoice: Your line: leave the corners. What's left standing is theirs to gather. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: thou shalt leave them for the poor and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God.
